figures.caption: Figure 1: From Single-Path Generation to Clinical Consensus Selection (CCS). (a) Conventional RRG systems ultimately return one decoded report as the final output; (b) CCS forms a candidate rollout pool and selects the report with higher relative clinical consensus.

Table 2: Evaluation results across radiology MLLM backbones and datasets. CCS uses Qwen3-VL-Embed as the clinical consensus utility. All rollout pools are generated with sampling temperature τ = 0.5 and pool size N = 8. “ ↑” and “ ↓” indicate changes relative to the corresponding sampling baseline. Within each “+ CCS” row, metrics are marked by the empirical distribution of relative changes δ = (CCS− baseline)/baseline: bold indicates upper-quartile gains (δ ≥ +4.17%), while underline indicates median-to-upper-quartile gains (δ ≥ +1.88%).

Table 7: Detailed hyperparameters for adapting Qwen3VL-Embed-2B for CXR–report representation learning. LoRA adapters are fine-tuned with a contrastive objective, using temperature τ and false-negative margin δ for embedding optimisation.

Table 3: Comparison of CCS with different consensus utilities. All utilities select from the same rollout pool, isolating the effect of the consensus scoring function. The ‘w/o fine-tuning’ variant is the original Qwen3-VL-Embed checkpoint before radiology-specific adaptation for RRG. The best result in each column is shown in bold.

Figure 3: Effect of rollout size under different utilities. Each subplot reports one metric as the sampling rollout size varies over N∈{2, 4, 8, 16} under different consensus utilities. Beam-search shows a similar trend in Figure 5.

Figure 2: Overview of the Clinical Consensus Selection framework. At inference time, CCS proceeds in four stages: (1) constructing a rollout pool from a radiology MLLM; (2) computing pairwise utilities among candidates; (3) aggregating them into relative consensus scores; and (4) selecting the final report according to relative consensus.

Figure 4: Utility decision-space clustermap at N=8. Pairwise Cohen’s κ measures agreement between utilities over per-sample candidate choices. Hierarchical clustering separates utility groups at κ=0.21.

Figure 5: Effect of rollout size under different utilities with beam search. Each subplot reports one metric as the beam-search rollout size varies over N∈{2, 4, 8, 16} under different consensus utilities.

Table 9: Ablation study of sampling temperature (τ ). Effect of sampling temperature on candidate generation for clinical consensus selection, where τ = 0 denotes greedy decoding. Best and second-best results are bolded and underlined, respectively. τ ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0}.

Table 1: Evaluation results on the MIMIC-CXR test split. All rollout-based methods select from the same candidate pool with N = 8, generated with identical MLLM settings, temperature, and random seed. p-values and 95% CIs compare our method against the Sampling baseline. The best result in each column is shown in bold.

Table 8: Prompt templates used in this work. The templates include both the report-generation prompt for MLLM rollout and the query/document prompts for Qwen3-VL-Embed representation learning and inference. The same templates are used consistently during training and inference unless otherwise specified.
